# Chart Lua ownership

`deadsync-song-lua` owns DeadSync's chart-Lua compatibility semantics. A theme
change must not change compilation, modifier windows, actor transforms, proxy
targets, capture ordering, or scheduled chart media.

- The compiler and `playback/prepare.rs` select song layers, preserve shared-session
  compilation and independent-layer fallback, and prepare runtime commands.
- `gameplay.rs` translates compiled commands into the deterministic windows
  consumed by `deadsync-gameplay`. The gameplay crate never depends on this
  presentation-aware crate and never builds actors.
- `playback.rs` owns actor execution, proxies, offscreen captures, media schedules,
  frame ordering, and song-lifetime scratch storage. It uses the existing
  `NoteskinSlot` contract, not the concrete asset loader or profile types.
- `deadsync-notefield` continues to own note rendering and player transform math.
- `deadsync-assets` supplies file/resource compilation. `deadsync-profile-gameplay`
  supplies profile/session compilation context. Neither supplies Lua semantics.
- `deadsync-shell` initiates preparation, coordinates media and warmup, and runs
  composition for gameplay and practice. Simply Love supplies presentation
  fragments through `frame_layers` and its existing field/HUD adapter. Shared
  playback decides which fragments a chart captures and how it transforms them.

The renderer reads gameplay state without advancing judgment or chart timing.
Buffers and caches retain their song lifetime and are prepared before live play.

Playback fixtures live in `tests/playback.rs`. They include the production source
so they can exercise private capture/cache paths with real asset slots without a
library-unit-test type-identity cycle through the asset crate. Full-frame gameplay
and practice regressions live with the shell orchestration. Native ITGmania actor
and Lua-semantic fixtures remain in the workspace tests.

The separately authorized [production migration](../../docs/testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-production-migration/objective.txt)
is in progress. The standalone interpreter and C API removal milestones remain
closed. The opt-in `rust-engine` feature exposes `rust_engine::RustSongRuntime`
through the shared `deadlib-lua` Rust host API. It owns clock/SongPosition and RNG
bindings, file/environment helpers, actor declarations, and the current
Actor/ActorFrame/ActorFrameTexture/Quad/Sprite/Banner/Sound/BitmapText/GraphDisplay/SongMeterDisplay/CourseContentsList/Model/ActorMultiVertex/ActorProxy
and wrapper instance bindings.
`Def` creates declarations; `instantiate_actor` creates a scene whose command,
tween and message lifecycle is driven through the runtime. Resource bindings
include retained texture handles, Sound and Sprite preparation events, and mesh
uploads with a renderer-facing read API. Proxy bindings retain target identity
and expose the existing player/screen/actor target classification for downstream
overlay resolution. ActorFrameTexture bindings own allocation requests and
retained texture metadata. Custom draw callbacks and explicit `Draw` submissions
produce immutable draw frames with nested render targets, caller transforms,
mesh payloads and the existing capture limits. The host resolves captured actor
identities through the compiler/playback source map.
BitmapText bindings include text conversion, attributes, stroke and layout
settings, font resolution, and the existing theme helpers. `LoadFont` creates
reusable text templates; concatenation preserves command composition and
independent mutable attributes. Text resource reads return owned payloads.
Complete compiler text-change capture/publication remains part of the pending
song integration.
The existing RollingNumbers, BPMDisplay, DeviceList and InputList classes now
instantiate with Actor inheritance and private text/numeric bindings. Their
formatting, bound receiver behavior and fixed input-status resource labels are
covered by production comparisons. Additional own methods on unlinked classes
remain part of the binding migration.

Banner inherits Sprite and has Rust bindings for its existing media loaders,
scrolling controls and size methods. The shared Sprite media helpers retain
path-query ordering, the per-actor current-background Lua helper, and the existing
texture reset/publication distinctions. The bundled blank bitmap is prepared by
one Lua-independent routine shared with the production control.

GraphDisplay owns its two body children and line child, with the existing named
lookup and command traversal rules. `Load` and `Set` preserve metric/stat fields,
life-record callbacks and fallback samples. `actor_graph_display` returns owned
sample and child-style data; compiler publication remains pending.

SongMeterDisplay materializes its Stream declaration, preserves its width methods
and exposes owned stream render data. Its stream initializes after the meter,
runs startup commands and joins the cached frame traversal. Named children share
one helper with GraphDisplay. Generated groups remain rooted while a callback
invalidates the update plan and collects; plan invalidation and scene retirement
release those roots. Full meter publication remains part of compiler integration.

CourseContentsList retains its raw or existing Display table, scroller fields,
transform callbacks and per-player SetSong parameters. Shared displays retain
identity across lists; scene ownership keeps their callbacks and later wrappers
alive until the last owning scene retires. Plain display tables keep their authored
methods and metatables. Production manager and compiler integration remain pending.

Model construction preserves its default depth, culling and texture settings,
Actor inheritance and private sprite/child-query methods. Resource reads resolve
Meshes/Materials/Bones and return owned layers through the existing asset loader.
Preparation uses the existing Rust material clocks, preserving state selection,
hibernation, parent update rates and callback ordering. Material samples survive
capture retirement; scene ownership retains frame data until release. Declared
camera FOV and its command override now initialize the Rust render state. Full
Model publication and live rendering remain part of compiler/playback integration.

PREFSMAN and DISPLAY now use Rust host bindings. Preferences retain their existing
defaults, case-sensitive stored overrides, receiver behavior and side-effect
ordering. Display specs and modes preserve shared identity across calls. Logical
screen dimensions stay independent of physical display preferences; the aspect
helper reads the current public preference store. Traced method captures keep
saved queries and values alive without retaining discarded manager cycles. The
unchanged display-size fixture checks these bindings with framebuffer allocation
and actor rendering state in preparation and live contexts.

THEME exposes the existing paths, localized strings, metric definitions and
dynamic SL metric lookups through Rust bindings. Numeric metric getters keep
their definition-only behavior; lead-in and scoring queries read the current SL
tables with normal metamethods and traced intermediate values. Virtual theme
paths load Actor, Sprite or Sound declarations without filesystem resolution,
preserving the production host's initial resource state. Theme font paths use
the existing owned bitmap-font resources.

SL state, ThemePrefs and SL_CustomPrefs are initialized in the Rust song host.
Per-player modifiers, stage statistics, streams and mode tables preserve the
production defaults and separate table identities. ThemePrefs retains a private
store; InitAll preserves existing values and evaluates default getters with the
existing side-effect and error rules. ParseChartInfo retains its target streams
across callback reentry and collection. ParseColumnCues uses the existing Lua
helper unchanged. Theme preference option-row UI bindings remain pending.

The Rust song host now installs SONGMAN and SongUtil using retained song, chart,
course and trail objects. Chart selection uses immutable authored metadata and
traced chart identities even when scripts change the exposed arrays or getters.
Timing queries retain their owned music-rate state; density stays cached at
construction while column cues invoke the current Steps timing callbacks.
Collecting and reentrant callbacks preserve their intermediate objects. The
catalog retains selection slots and option groups for compiler/live integration.

SongOptions now has distinct Preferred, Stage, Song and Current objects. Setters,
text parsing and assignment, stage restart, attack clearing and the song phase of
current-option approach preserve the existing values, identities and write order.
Timing queries retain the same Current object as those updates. Group operations
remain explicit host phases; GAMESTATE methods use the same retained option levels.

The catalog also owns eight PlayerOptions objects, one per player and level.
Rust bindings preserve lazy methods, mutable state/speed tables, perspective
aliases, speed modes, string parsing, timing-window controls and noteskin callback
dispatch. Saved methods retain the appropriate owner across GC and observe
replaced state on later calls. PlayerState now retains these levels and distinct
SongPosition wrappers, provides option strings/arrays, and assigns options with
the native propagation and partial-failure order.

Host option phases preserve the chronological clock, stage restart, attack
rebuilding/clearing and SongOptions/PREFSMAN/player update order. Position queries
and sampling do not advance options. Controller and health queries read values
published by the host; the complete live health-update and message-dispatch phase
still needs migration. GAMESTATE exposes PlayerState and option methods.

The song-side NOTESKIN manager uses the existing resolver through
`RustSongRuntime::new_with_noteskin_resolver`. It snapshots song-local skin names,
provides typed metrics and paths, compiles metric commands, and loads Lua templates
with independent skin/button/element environments. Image and missing-resource
templates have native actor methods and independent concatenation state. Saved
commands retain their environments across collection and scene phases. The Var
fallback and its GameCommand queries use the current public GAMESTATE methods.

PROFILEMAN now provides the existing machine, player, fallback and local profile
objects through Rust bindings. Saved methods retain their original owner, mutable
user tables preserve identity, and setters keep conversion and side-effect order.
High-score lists expose the existing defaults and resolve current score-name
callbacks while preserving list mutation and collection during lookup. Profile
cycles are traced by the VM.

STATSMAN provides the existing stage and player statistics through Rust bindings.
Host reset and frame-feed phases preserve selected-step and table identities,
partial writes on errors, and recorded life versus current meter life. Live-player
publication is a separate phase; FailPlayer updates published state and queues
ordered writes when live mode is active. Saved queries retain only their required
objects. Full live orchestration and its query tracing still need migration.

GAMESTATE now exposes the production method surface through the writable GameState
class table and its protected instance metatable. Selection setters retain private
slots and immutable chart metadata, broadcast CurrentSteps changes synchronously,
and re-read the selected chart after callbacks before updating other players.
Preference reads, modifier queries/commands, environment values, style and clock
helpers retain their existing argument, side-effect and error behavior. Message
delivery and guarded ScriptError reporting share the actor host's implementation.
The frozen current-option controls and song-options-string fixture now exercise
the installed GAMESTATE methods. Compiler capture and screen-transition/live
orchestration still need migration.

GAMEMAN, CHARMAN, MEMCARDMAN, UNLOCKMAN and HOOKS now use Rust host bindings.
They retain the existing sandbox policies, including GAMEMAN's fresh single-style
list and the side-effect counters for manager operations. Unlock mutators chain
to their original owner; independent queries and style getters retain only the
data they need. These bindings do not introduce platform operations.

Generated gameplay actors, remaining managers/input, complete compiler capture
and live scenes still need migration. The production song compiler uses the legacy
engine until the complete replacement and its downstream behavior are verified.
This opt-in component is not the production cutover. See the
[migration ledger](../../docs/testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-production-migration/README.md)
and [architecture contract](../../docs/lua-architecture.md).

# Lua architecture and delivery contract

Accepted direction: 2026-11-03; scope corrected by the user on 2026-11-04.
This is the architecture contract for future Lua
work. [lua-engine.md](lua-engine.md) records implementation status and historical
evidence; [lua-cache.md](lua-cache.md) describes the existing program cache.
When older progress notes describe a different work order, this contract governs
future work. The diagram describes the target, not a claim that it is implemented.

## Objective and priorities

**Current user-requested scope: migrate every existing production Lua consumer
to `deadlib-lua`.** The separately authorized production migration explicitly
supersedes the earlier "integration deferred" instruction. Its fixed scope and
evidence are recorded in the [migration ledger](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-production-migration/README.md)
and [verbatim objective](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-production-migration/objective.txt).
The migration is in progress: song production still uses the legacy backend.
Noteskin preparation and Simply Love's GIF loader now use the shared Rust engine.
Noteskin regression and baseline comparisons pass; final downstream and
application validation remain pending.
Completion requires the full song, live callback, noteskin and GIF paths to use
the shared Rust engine, preserve existing supported behavior, pass application
validation and remove legacy from normal/build dependencies. Stop at those
criteria; new StepMania features, baking capabilities and language parity work
are separate requests.

The interpreter milestone is complete for its recorded source snapshot. The
separate removal goal is also complete: Lua C API/ABI compatibility was removed
while preserving the interpreter and Rust host API. Its verified finish line is normal Rust-only builds, no
Lua C interface in production artifacts, applicable regression checks with no
unexplained new failures, and matching active tooling/documentation. Unrelated
interpreter defects do not keep that removal goal open. Performance expansion
is deferred. Both milestones remain closed; the new migration has its own
explicit authorization and does not reopen either milestone.

Build an independent Lua engine in Rust with Lua 5.1 language semantics, shared
eventually by song and noteskin integrations through a Rust host API. DeadSync does not
require a drop-in implementation of Lua's C API. C ABI compatibility, loading
third-party Lua C modules, C-specific continuation behavior, `lua_Alloc` parity
and private C-runtime T/testC helpers are permanently excluded from the supported engine interface. They do not
gate the Rust engine or its DeadSync integrations. This correction supersedes
the earlier standalone C-compatibility completion requirement.

Both integrations depend directly on the shared engine:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DeadSync --> Song["deadsync-song-lua"]
    DeadSync --> Noteskin["deadsync-noteskin"]
    Song --> API["deadlib-lua: Rust host API"]
    Noteskin --> API
    API --> Core["Rust parser/compiler, bytecode VM, GC and standard library"]
```

The engine implements Lua; the adapters implement song, actor and noteskin
behavior. Use the pinned PUC interpreter as a test oracle for relevant Lua
semantics without depending on it for production execution. Rust API ownership,
error handling and resource behavior need their own explicit contract; exact
PUC C-stack layouts and allocation sequences are not that contract.

The preferred gameplay path is ahead-of-time
scene baking: perform eligible Lua work during preparation and play the resulting
native scene without repeating that Lua work every frame. Live execution and
hybrid execution are first-class capabilities for behavior that remains dynamic.

Measure representative preparation, live execution and memory against the
recorded production baseline. Earlier LuaJIT performance aspirations are not
acceptance criteria for this migration. Measure runtime execution separately
from the end-to-end gains of existing scene baking.

Correct Lua 5.1 behavior is mandatory across execution strategies and backends.
Later Lua 5.2-5.5 dialects remain an extension goal, but must not displace the 5.1,
scene-baking and live-execution work. Keep one shared compiler/runtime foundation.

## Target pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Song["Song Lua scripts"] --> Frontend
    Noteskin["Noteskin Lua scripts"] --> Frontend
    subgraph Engine["deadlib-lua: independent Rust engine"]
        Frontend["Lexer + parser + compiler"] --> Verified["Verified Lua bytecode"]
        Verified --> Optimize["Low-level optimizer + verification"]
        Optimize --> Program["Cached compiled program"]
        Program --> VM["Fast register VM"]
        Program -.-> Native["Optional native machine code"]
        VM <--> Memory["Shared VM memory: tables, closures, upvalues, GC"]
        Native <--> Memory
    end
    VM --> Host["Rust host API"]
    Native --> Host
    subgraph SongIntegration["deadsync-song-lua"]
        SongAPI["Song API + actor commands + timing"] --> Strategy{"Execution strategy: Auto by default"}
        Strategy --> Bake["Ahead-of-time scene baking: preferred"]
        Strategy --> Hybrid["Hybrid: baked data + live callbacks"]
        Strategy --> Live["Live Lua execution"]
    end
    subgraph NoteskinIntegration["deadsync-noteskin"]
        NoteskinAPI["Noteskin API + assets + actor construction"] --> NoteskinData["Compiled noteskin data + dynamic callbacks"]
    end
    Host --> SongAPI
    Host --> NoteskinAPI
    Bake --> Scene["Native DeadSync scene + renderer"]
    Hybrid --> Scene
    Live --> Scene
    NoteskinData --> Scene
```

The engine owns language semantics, bytecode, optimization, execution, objects,
GC and Rust host-call boundaries. The integrations own their domain APIs, dependency
capture, scene construction, baking policy and renderer-facing data. Song and
noteskin support must reuse the engine rather than grow separate Lua evaluators.

The diagram's earlier "Pure Rust" label means an independently owned engine,
without delegating execution to a linked C Lua/LuaJIT runtime. It is not a ban on
unsafe Rust, intrinsics, inline assembly, assembly backends or necessary platform
FFI. Platform FFI is distinct from the removed Lua C compatibility interface.
Keep the portable interpreter available on supported targets. Native code
is optional to run the engine; its absence must not disable scene baking.

## Independent stages and artifacts

| Stage | Contract | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compile | Parse source or import supported native chunks without executing the user's program. | Verified, VM-independent program. |
| Optimize | Transform that program while preserving the selected Lua semantics, including observable errors, hooks and numeric behavior. Verify transformed code. | Reusable optimized program and execution metadata. |
| Execute | Run through the register VM or a supported native backend, using the same object model and host-call contract. | Lua values and host effects. |
| Bake | Execute/analyze eligible host behavior against an explicit preparation environment and convert it to native scene operations. | Scene/noteskin artifact, dependency manifest and any residual live callbacks. |
| Play | Evaluate the native scene and run residual callbacks only where needed. | Native scene updates and renderer input. |

Ahead-of-time **scene baking** produces scene data: actor structures, assets,
timelines, curves, commands and supported parameterized operations. Ahead-of-time
**machine-code compilation** produces executable code. They are separate choices;
the baker can use the interpreter or native backend, and live execution can use
either backend. Caching bytecode alone does not constitute scene baking.

Expose independently testable compile, optimize and bake stages with explicit
inputs and identities. Prefer evaluating native curves and commands over storing
an unbounded per-frame trace. Account for bake time and artifact size as well as
playback cost; preparation can happen at load time or earlier when inputs exist.

## Execution strategies and equivalence

`Auto` is the intended default policy. It prefers full baking when equivalence
can be established, otherwise hybrid execution, otherwise live execution. Expose
explicit live, bake and hybrid selection for validation and diagnosis. A forced
bake that cannot cover the requested behavior must explain the unsupported
dependency; it must not silently discard behavior or call a hybrid result baked.
Selection names here describe the contract, not an existing public API.

Bake deterministic work whose dependencies are known or can be represented as
native runtime inputs. Time-dependent behavior can become a native timeline or
curve if it preserves the required clock semantics. Player actions, mutable
external state, messages and unknown callbacks must remain dynamic unless their
behavior is faithfully represented in the scene. One recorded playthrough or a
few sampled frames cannot establish equivalence for all future inputs.

Live, baked and hybrid paths must agree on actor identity and hierarchy, command
and message ordering, callback effects, timing and beat conversions, tweens,
randomness, errors and visible rendering behavior. Cover seeks, rate changes,
stops/warps, pause/resume and event boundaries. Preserve evaluation order and
numeric behavior under the pinned reference contract; record any allowed
rendering tolerance explicitly rather than silently approximating Lua results.
Validate the new live path against the existing legacy/ITGmania host-semantic
tests as well: agreement between two new strategies can conceal a shared bug.

Interpreter/native transitions within a running state share tables, closures,
upvalues, environments, userdata and GC ownership. Hybrid execution must preserve
that identity with the residual callbacks. Cached immutable programs may be
shared across independent VMs; mutable Lua objects must not be shared accidentally
between unrelated instances or reconstructed as disconnected copies at a handoff.

Baking and fallback must not duplicate initialization, RNG consumption, messages,
file/network writes or other externally visible effects. Capture/model effects
where possible; leave unsupported effects on the live path. Establish a valid
handoff or restart boundary before exposing effects. If dependencies change,
invalidate/rebuild or fall back with defined state continuity, not by silently
re-running an already published portion of the script.

## Cache identities

Keep three artifact classes distinct: compiled programs, optional native code,
and baked scenes/noteskins. The current [ProgramCache](lua-cache.md) implements
only the first class. A program cache hit does not prove a scene cache hit.

Scene identity must cover the program and transitive script/module dependencies,
asset identities, chart/song timing, relevant preferences and player configuration,
RNG policy/state, host API and baker versions, and every captured environmental
input. Record dependencies actually used; unknown or untracked inputs prevent
reuse unless they remain explicit runtime inputs. Native artifacts additionally
bind backend/ABI/CPU features and numeric/code-generation settings.

Persist stable scene data and bindings, not raw VM IDs, pointers or live closure
addresses. Residual callback reconstruction must preserve its declared state and
identity relationships. Reject stale/incompatible artifacts and rebuild from
authoritative inputs. Validate cache hits, misses and invalidation against the
same uncached semantics, including changed dependencies and fresh processes.

## Performance implementation policy

Study [LuaJIT's interpreter and tracing compiler](https://luajit.org/luajit.html)
and [source](https://github.com/LuaJIT/LuaJIT/tree/v2.1). Source reuse/adaptation,
unsafe Rust, SIMD/intrinsics, inline assembly and dedicated assembly paths are
explicitly permitted where justified. Record upstream revision and provenance
and retain applicable copyright/license notices for reused code. The aim is
performance with maintainable correctness, not a restriction to safe Rust syntax.

Isolate target-specific paths with documented memory/ABI/GC invariants, CPU feature
selection and a tested portable fallback. Test optimized and fallback paths on
their supported targets. Representation changes, dispatch specialization, guarded
lookup caches, host-call inlining and native compilation are candidates; choose
them using profiles and measured workloads rather than an assumed benefit.

The compatibility oracle remains the pinned PUC Lua 5.1.5 build described in
[the reference contract](lua-engine.md#reference-contract). LuaJIT's documented
[extensions and differences](https://luajit.org/extensions.html), including RNG,
numeric conversion, yielding and bytecode, are not permission to change that
contract. Native optimization must preserve floating-point evaluation, error and
debug behavior, GC roots/barriers and execution limits. Guard and fall back where
a backend cannot preserve them.

Benchmark the current implementation, PUC Lua 5.1, LuaJIT interpreter mode and
LuaJIT JIT mode on pinned, identical supported inputs. Record versions, build
flags, CPU/OS, warmup, cache state and exact output checks; rotate/interleave runs
and retain raw results. Report both cold and warmed execution, startup, compile/
bake cost, allocations, peak/live memory, artifact size and representative scales.
Measure p95/p99/worst observed frame times, GC and compilation pauses as well as
throughput. Label unsupported workloads and semantic differences explicitly.

Keep VM-only comparisons separate from scene preparation/playback comparisons.
An accepted scene optimization must demonstrate less playback work while retaining
correctness and reporting preparation/memory costs. The runtime goal remains to
exceed LuaJIT on relevant live workloads; do not claim universal superiority
from selected wins or require a JIT where baking already removes the work.

## Delivery gates and work order

The standalone Rust Lua engine milestone has its own completed report. The
completed removal goal preserves the applicable language, library, GC, ownership,
errors and Rust API contracts against the pinned oracle and direct Rust tests.
Lua C compatibility is permanently unsupported. Adapter and migration work
belongs to the separately authorized production migration, not to either closed
goal. Its acceptance scope is fixed by the objective linked above. Later project
milestones do not extend it or reopen the interpreter milestone.

| Milestone | Evidence required before declaring it complete |
| --- | --- |
| Rust Lua 5.1 engine | Parser/compiler, VM, GC, Lua-visible standard library and applicable debug/coroutine behavior have current-source tests against the pinned oracle. The Rust host API has tested ownership, handles, callbacks, errors and resource behavior. Run applicable language/library suites and adversarial tests; explain reference failures and capability exclusions. C API conformance, private T/testC and C-specific continuations are not required. |
| Shared integration (active migration) | Port existing host bindings, callbacks, ownership and renderer-facing behavior to the Rust host API. Opt-in components are intermediate evidence; the final production paths must use the shared engine unconditionally. |
| Scene baking | Preserve existing preparation, baking, live execution and fallback semantics during migration, with baseline output comparisons and cache correctness. New baking capabilities require a separate request. |
| Project performance targets (deferred) | The migration reports representative before/after preparation time, live cost and memory. Broader optimization, native-code work and LuaJIT performance targets are outside its acceptance scope. |
| Production migration (active) | Every inventoried Lua consumer uses the Rust engine; existing supported behavior passes applicable regressions; the normal app builds and renders correctly without an engine flag or legacy normal/build dependency; documentation and validation accurately describe that state. Any fallback uses the Rust engine. |

Passing a selected song corpus alone does not establish Lua language correctness.
Do not replace scene baking with a faster interpreter. Runtime/compiler investment
must support both the baker and the live path. Native-code work may remain
experimental until its own correctness/performance evidence is sufficient.

## Current implementation boundary

The production migration is active and separate from the completed interpreter
and C API-removal milestones. The earlier unfinished actor-instance experiment
was preserved under
`analysis/lua/deferred-actor-instances-2026-11-04/` and removed from the active
crate. Its last run passed eight tests and failed one; it is not validated work.
The prior adapter snapshot's 244 recorded source hashes were restored exactly
before the separately authorized migration. That archive is historical evidence,
not the implementation used by the current migration tests.

The independent compiler, register VM, GC, standard library, program cache and
Rust host API remain. The separate removal deletes the former partial C ABI;
it is not retained as an optional feature. Historical C-compatibility counts
cannot establish Rust integration readiness. `deadsync-song-lua` still depends
on the workspace's `mlua` alias for `deadlib-lua-legacy` in production.
`deadsync-noteskin` now unconditionally uses the Rust engine through
`compiler::compile_data`, including cache preparation. Compiler version 30
invalidates version-29 cache identities. Its legacy compiler is isolated in
test/example support with a dev dependency; there is no noteskin engine flag.
The current migration ledger records 312 passing noteskin tests and comparisons.
The earlier
[noteskin corpus checks](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-noteskin-corpus.md) cover all
bundled skins and six committed regression skins. Song Lua now has an initial
[Rust clock/RNG component](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-song-clock.md) with focused
Windows release and Linux x64 controls.
The [Rust file loader](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-song-loader.md) now preserves
song script environments and nested file context. The
[actor declaration adapter](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-actor-definitions.md)
adds `Def`, declaration composition and template `LoadActor` through that API.
The current opt-in song host also owns Actor/ActorFrame/ActorFrameTexture/Quad/Sprite/Banner/Sound/BitmapText/ActorMultiVertex/ActorProxy instances,
commands, tween queues, messages, render properties, effect clocks and wrapper

compare the existing production bindings; full compiler output and movie playback
still require downstream validation.

ActorProxy bindings retain target tables through traced captures and ordinary

mesh geometry and nested render targets. The Rust host and legacy control share
the existing Lua-independent frame format and source conversion. Whole-song
compiler scheduling, manual draw state projection into compiled actors and final

including reusable `LoadFont` templates and their declaration concatenation.
Owned text payloads survive GC and scene retirement; complete text-change
capture/publication into compiled and live overlays still requires integration.
RollingNumbers, BPMDisplay, DeviceList and InputList construction and text/numeric
bindings preserve Actor inheritance, retained private methods and the existing
rolling-number formatting and input-status labels. Additional own methods on

scrolling controls and size methods. The shared Sprite media helpers retain
path-query ordering, the per-actor current-background Lua helper, and the existing

GraphDisplay now has Rust construction, native body/line children, `Load`/`Set`
bindings and an owned render payload. Named-child aliases, command traversal,
life-record callbacks and fallback samples follow the existing production host.
Complete graph publication still depends on the pending compiler integration.
SongMeterDisplay has Rust stream construction, width methods and owned resource
reads, including the existing stream Init/startup/update ordering. Graph and meter
bindings share named-child lookup. Cached traversal groups are traced through

Compiler publication and full live-screen integration remain pending.

CourseContentsList retains Display identity, including plain declarations and
existing text actors, and implements its existing scroller and SetFromGameState
bindings. Shared display ownership spans scenes and includes wrappers added later.
SetSong parameter construction resolves the current GAMESTATE methods at each
call; complete production manager bindings remain a separate unfinished part of
this same migration.

Model construction now preserves its native render defaults and private sprite
and child-query methods. Meshes/Materials/Bones resolution feeds the existing

ordering. Captures own their frame data until drained or released with the scene.

PREFSMAN and DISPLAY have Rust manager bindings, including preference mutation,

column cues call the current Lua timing getters with intermediate values rooted

for compiler/live integration; the normal production song path is still legacy.

values, partial writes on errors, text parsing, level assignment, restart, attack
clearing and song-option approach. Captured level references remain independent
of mutable public test aliases. Chronological group operations remain explicit

for both players. Lazy methods keep their native cache and receiver rules while

and preserve writes preceding a callback or side-effect failure. High-score lists
retain their own mutable arrays, traverse raw sequence entries, and invoke the

and updates the current raw player array; frame publication updates the original

writes. FailPlayer updates published live players and appends ordered host writes
only during live execution. These explicit host phases remain separate from clock,

wrapper. GetPlayerOptionsString/Array preserve native formatting and return fresh
arrays; SetPlayerOptions preserves Current-first assignment, table identity and
partial writes on failure. Host option phases perform stage restart, attack
rebuilding/clearing and chronological updates. Each update advances SongOptions,
calls the current PREFSMAN getter, then advances each player's Current values with
its own frame delta. The clock commits before those callbacks, preserving reentry
and failure behavior. Position sampling remains independent of option updates.
Controller and health getters read host-published status without running update
phases. Live health calculation and HealthStateChanged dispatch remain part of the
unfinished live-scene migration. GAMESTATE methods and explicit host phases use
the same retained PlayerState and option objects.

GAMESTATE's production method surface is installed through a writable GameState
class table, with a protected instance metatable and normal instance overrides.
Song, style, trail, Steps and sort selections retain private slots independently
of public getters and catalog aliases. SetCurrentSteps validates immutable chart
metadata, broadcasts synchronously even for the same selected pointer, then
re-reads the selection before applying the existing other-player policy. Failed
callbacks preserve earlier writes. Missing-chart diagnostics use the actor host's
guarded ScriptError delivery. Environment, display-BPM/layout, controller and
clock helpers preserve their existing getter/receiver rules. Game commands retain
their one-based numeric player convention and authored clause order; modifier
queries compare copies against Current options. The unchanged native option
assertions exercise these methods through their public APIs. Screen-transition
selection initialization and the full compiler/live orchestration remain pending.

GAMEMAN, CHARMAN, MEMCARDMAN, UNLOCKMAN and HOOKS preserve the existing sandbox
policies through Rust host bindings. GAMEMAN returns a fresh single-style list
independently of session style; style columns retain the existing argument and
clamping rules. Manager operations preserve side-effect counting, errors and
chaining to retained owners. Query captures do not retain unnecessary manager
cycles, and all returned mutable lists are fresh.

The [migration ledger](testing/2026-11-04-rust-lua-production-migration/README.md)
records their differential checks and limitations. Generated gameplay actors,
remaining manager/input/media bindings, full captured output and live scenes,
production song cutover and final application validation remain required.
The engine exposes Rust host functions, captured binding data, rooted values and
protected table operations. The existing song integration already contains
native compilation/baking and live facilities; use those as integration inputs
and regression controls rather than assuming no prior work exists.

The active migration ports bindings and retained Lua values to that Rust API. The song
adapter also uses direct `mlua::ffi` stack access, including `src/raw_vm.rs`;

but that is not the chosen migration strategy. Preserve the adapters' Lua-visible
behavior and validate real scripts, callbacks and renderer-facing output against
the legacy path. Engine changes should supply shared language/runtime operations;
actor, timing, asset and noteskin policy stays in the adapter crates.

The shared independent-engine integration, public stage boundaries, native-code
backend and scene artifact/cache contract are target work. No separate
`deadsync-noteskin-lua` crate is required by this design. Track their status
separately from the legacy implementation's
capabilities. Update [lua-engine.md](lua-engine.md) with current evidence as each
gate closes; historical test counts or benchmark reports are not current proof.

# Production Lua migration: fixed acceptance scope

The [verbatim user objective](objective.txt) is authoritative. This is a new,
explicitly authorized integration milestone. The interpreter and C API removal
milestones remain closed. This ledger records incomplete work; it is not a
completion report.

## Frozen baseline

`baseline-sources.json` records SHA-256 hashes of 16,404 parent-repository files.
`baseline-copies.json` identifies the 1,289 source/configuration files preserved
under `target/rust-lua-production-before`. The fixture submodule is recorded
separately in `fixtures.json` and `fixture-sources.json`: 3,980 files at
`f896283ab5e3a861ba8517569f156b1b34fa2ab6`, with local status preserved. No missing
whole-song resources were downloaded or replaced with a different chart.

`inventory.json` records the three direct production consumers, ten downstream
packages, 84 source files referencing Lua handles, 384 raw/identity access sites,
and 949 retained-handle field/parameter candidates. These are conservative
source candidates, including inline tests and performance controls; each must
be classified during migration. Package dependency kinds establish the
production edges. `production-tree.stdout` preserves the original normal/build
dependency graph. Historical reports are not final-source evidence.

The previous C API removal verification script referenced by earlier chat is
absent from the current worktree. Its unavailable invocation is preserved in
`prior-removal-verifier.stderr`; it is not being recreated or used to reopen that
completed milestone.

## Requirements and evidence needed

| Requirement | Acceptance evidence | Current status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All production consumers inventoried | Manifest edges, source references, raw calls and retained handles in `inventory.json` | Initial inventory recorded; classify every candidate during implementation |
| Fixed supported behavior and fixtures | Frozen source/fixture hashes, existing regression commands, whole-song resource identities | Recorded; harness repaired; interim song run has 1,130 passes and one documented pre-existing renderer/test mismatch |
| Full production song path | Actor/method/command/manager/input/message/media/clock/RNG/file/baking/live regression results and frozen output comparisons | Pending; existing Rust adapter covers only part of this surface |
| Noteskin preparation and callbacks | All bundled and regression skin output comparisons plus downstream assets/rendering tests | Unconditional Rust engine; 312 tests pass with unchanged sources; downstream rendering pending |
| GIF and other production consumers | All bundled GIF definitions and existing behavior tests; no remaining production legacy consumers | GIF loader switched unconditionally; 112 isolated comparisons and 15 production tests pass; final-source run pending |
| Ordering, shared state, errors and sandbox | Applicable existing tests and differential checks, including callback reentry and all original limits | GIF bounded execution and initial actor comparisons pass; full song integration pending |
| Root ownership and teardown | Forced GC while retaining callbacks, reentry, reload, session destruction and thread ownership checks | Pending full production paths |
| Core/domain separation | Generic core facilities only; actor/song/noteskin/GIF policy remains in owning crates | Required for every change |
| Existing preparation/live/fallback semantics | Production preparation and live-scene tests; every fallback uses the Rust engine | Pending |
| Cache correctness | Versioned/incompatible artifact invalidation with cache regression results | Noteskin version 30 and old-cache replacement verified; song integration pending |
| Unconditional normal engine | Normal application build, normal/build dependency tree, build/link evidence without legacy or experimental flags | Pending |
| Remove duplicate production backends | Final source/manifests/tooling audit; any legacy oracle isolated to dev/test use | Pending |
| Final-source regressions | Core, adapters and applicable downstream tests; all failures explained or fixed without removing coverage | Pending |
| Actual application smoke | Song loading, gameplay and rendered noteskins through normal application, with artifact/screenshots | Preserved legacy app rendered successfully; migrated application validation pending |
| Formatting and Clippy | Applicable checks against final source; platform gaps explicitly reported | Pending |
| Before/after preparation, live and memory | Preserved baseline binaries, matched inputs, raw measurements and allocation/RSS scope | Song baseline and paired production noteskin timing recorded; migrated song/live/memory measurements pending |
| Accurate active documentation | Final architecture/status/validation match production code | Architecture authorization updated; final report pending |

Completion requires every row to be proven. Passing only the interpreter, one
adapter, a headless smoke, or a dependency-tree check does not complete this goal.

## Baseline regression results

Commands and source hashes are retained in each check directory. The current
verified results are:

- `baseline-core-linux-debug`: 938 tests passed, source hashes unchanged.
- `baseline-noteskin-linux-debug`: 298 tests passed, source hashes unchanged.
- `baseline-song-windows-release`: compile failure before tests, source hashes
  unchanged. `actor_input_render` includes `playback/prepare_tests.rs`, whose
  `crate::tests::init_paths()` does not exist in that integration test crate.
  Repair the shared test initialization and rerun the full suite. Do not remove
  the included preparation tests or the rendering test to obtain a pass.
- `baseline-gifs-windows-release`: all 15 existing GIF tests passed, source
  hashes unchanged.
- The normal Windows application baseline Cargo build succeeded. The wrapper
  reported source changes in the independent core, which was outside that
  build's dependency graph. `baseline-application-windows-release/dependency-source-audit.json`
  records the dependency-file check and preserved executable hash. The original
  wrapper result remains unchanged. This is build evidence, not rendering smoke.

`checks.py` records complete commands, logs, environment, source hashes, elapsed
time and exit status. It refuses to overwrite an existing check directory.

## Performance and runtime workloads

`build_workloads.py` builds and preserves the existing `song_lua_execution`
normal shell binary, the `song_lua_performance` preparation example and the
noteskin `compare_lua_engines` example. The normal shell binary is built
separately from example/dev dependency feature unification. Each executable has
its own retained hash. Matched before/after runs must use the same fixtures and
configuration; preparation and live timing remain separate.

Measure both Rust allocation counters and process memory where available:
legacy Lua's C allocations are outside Rust global allocator counters, so those
counters alone cannot establish total memory parity. Record this distinction
with the raw measurements. Use the existing application `--perf-case` support
for actual rendering validation, separately from the headless live harness.

The initial Linux workload snapshot command accidentally traversed nested
ignored `target` directories. Its verified Python process was terminated before
starting Cargo, and the runner now enumerates the frozen source manifest. The
first filtered invocation failed because a non-login WSL command lacked Cargo
on PATH. The subsequent `baseline-pathfixed` invocation uses the login shell.
These are harness failures, not application results.

Linux production workload builds also needed D-Bus and systemd development
metadata. `linux_native_deps.py` downloaded pinned Debian packages into the
existing isolated prefix; package hashes are in `linux-native-deps.json`. No
system packages were installed. `baseline-dbus` successfully built and preserved
the normal headless live binary and preparation example, with source hashes
unchanged (`baseline-dbus-workloads-linux-debug/changed-sources.json`).
The noteskin comparison executable was preserved by `baseline-native`.

`baseline-noteskin-adapter.json` verifies complete native output equality for all
26 bundled dance/pump skins, with three comparison pairs per skin. This was a
debug build run alongside compilation: its timings are functional-run records,
not the requested release performance comparison. Before/after release timings
and process memory measurements remain pending.

The `pulse-driver` and `late-wrapper` microfixtures produced prepared actors but
no retained VM under the unchanged production backend. The live harness rejects
such baked-only cases by design; both raw reports are preserved as
`baseline-live-*.json`. They are not new migration failures and must not motivate
forcing otherwise eligible scenes into live execution. The full Cursed Metamorph
song also prepared into native actors and was rejected by this live-only harness;
`baseline-live-cursed-v2-linux-debug` records its ten input hashes, output and
99,233,792-byte process peak RSS. Selecting a supported interactive/input-dependent
source for the retained-callback baseline remains required. The existing
production fallback selects live execution on the explicit input-runtime request;
ordinary successful compilation preserves native playback.
Bad Trails registers `AddInputCallback` in its existing `lua/game.lua`; its
71-file input snapshot and retained-callback baseline run are under
`baseline-live-bad-trails-linux-debug`. It completed with a retained VM, 481
updates and no Lua errors, but only one visual change, failing the existing
live harness assertion. That failed baseline is preserved; the assertion was
not weakened. The script waits for input to advance its game.

`baseline-live-dreaming-windows-release` passed the same unchanged harness for
DREAMING-ING!!: retained VM, 481 updates, three changed visual frames, no Lua
errors and 92,045,312-byte peak working set. Its 25 input hashes are pinned.
`baseline-prepare-dreaming-windows-release` records three preparation samples
(1.3652, 1.3332 and 1.3354 seconds), the compiled output hash, and an
80,695,296-byte peak working set. Both used preserved legacy executables.
These runs overlapped compilation; controlled before/after timing comparisons
remain required. Windows memory now uses GetProcessMemoryInfo high-water
working-set and commit counters, plus private-byte samples.

All three Windows workload executables were built and preserved successfully.
Their wrapper also reported independent-core changes;
`baseline-workloads-windows-release/dependency-source-audit.json` distinguishes
the unchanged normal song binaries from the comparison tool's interim Rust
adapter. The latter's Rust side is not final-source evidence.
The first Cursed invocation lost the path suffix through nested shell quoting
and was stopped during input enumeration, before launching the application.
The runner now rejects nonexistent executables/simfiles before enumeration;
the replacement passes the complete path directly to WSL and pins ten files.

## Work in progress

The GIF replacement in `step_stats_gifs/rust_engine.rs` is now the unconditional
production capture implementation. The old implementation and direct legacy
dependency were removed from the theme crate. The song dependency still brings
legacy into the application; the overall cutover is incomplete.
`gif_probe.py` builds an isolated comparison against the exact
frozen capture implementation; its enum shims represent only the two player and
clock variants used by capture. The probe uses bounded VMs and checks oversized
runtime strings/tables, but is not final theme or application validation.

The comparison exposed and fixed an integer-overflow conversion difference:
the legacy Lua 5.1 bridge distinguishes exact integers from other numbers when
converting frame indices. The current probe passes 28 cases, each under both
players and aspect ratios (112 comparisons), including all 12 bundled scripts,
callback ordering, forced GC/reentry, numeric conversion, sandbox globals and
runaway root/callback scripts. Raw per-attempt results and source hashes are in
`gif-probe-runs`. Failed attempts remain recorded.

The generic core now offers a bounded VM and compilation through that VM's
budget. State buffers, retained parser roots, scratch strings and loaded
programs are charged to their owning domain. Compiler and bytecode-export
workspaces conservatively charge allocation requests through job completion;
streaming loads retain those charges across reader calls without activating
the workspace around Lua/host callbacks. Nine focused tests pass, covering
initialization, alignment, retained programs, runtime strings/tables, loadstring,
reader reentry, loadfile, bytecode dumping and recovery after memory errors.
This is not a process-RSS bound; caller-owned source, opaque Rust binding data
and operating-system resources are outside it.

The first broad run, `bounded-loading-owned-core-linux-debug`, exposed an
existing protected-error invariant after loader storage became VM-owned.
The loader now obtains the first reader result before allocating parser state,
so an already-raised reader memory error is returned without another allocation.
The original failing test passes unchanged; the full rerun under
`bounded-loading-fixed-core-linux-debug` passed all 947 tests with source hashes
unchanged (including the original 938 tests and nine new budget tests).

The first strict all-target Clippy invocation stopped on three existing legacy
oracle warnings (`manual_range_patterns`, `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks` and
`unused_enumerate_index`). Its log is `bounded-loading-clippy-linux.log`.
A `--no-deps --all-targets -- -D warnings` check now passes for the Rust core
(`bounded-loading-clippy-fixed-linux.log`). A new test's `err().expect()` was
changed to an explicit match; the test assertions and production code were
unchanged. The legacy oracle warnings remain recorded separately.

The missing song-test initialization was moved verbatim into
`tests/support/paths.rs` and shared by both playback integration crates. No
preparation or rendering tests were removed. The queued Windows baseline rerun
under `baseline-repaired-song-windows-release` failed compilation after the
noteskin manifest changed while it waited for the target lock: Cargo had
resolved the old optional dependency graph. It is not a backend behavior result.
The fresh `song-after-noteskin-song-windows-release` invocation completed with
1,130 tests passed, one failure and 43 existing ignored tests. The failure is
`song_lua_actor_multi_vertex_builds_textured_mesh_overlay`: the renderer replaces
glow RGBA with `[1; 4]`, while the assertion expects the source alpha. Both the
renderer and test exactly match the frozen baseline. This direct native overlay
test executes no Lua. `glow-baseline-audit.json` records the hashes and source
analysis; neither the renderer nor its failing assertion was changed. This is
a pre-existing source mismatch, not an executed frozen-baseline test result.
The run's broad source hashes changed during Rust actor work, so it remains
interim evidence. The original wrapper counted 916 tests in passing binaries;
the audit includes the additional 214 passes in the failing playback binary.
Future wrapper reports count passes in both successful and failing binaries.
`gif-cutover-gifs-windows-release` passed all 15 production tests; its wrapper
reported source changes during the run (noteskin cutover and core test lint fix).
This remains interim evidence, not a final-source application check.

## Noteskin production cutover

`compiler::compile_data` now always uses the shared Rust engine. The engine
feature and duplicate production compiler were removed. The normal/build tree
in `noteskin-cutover-normal-tree.stdout` contains `deadlib-lua` and no legacy
runtime. Legacy is a dev dependency used only by `tests/support/legacy.rs`,
historical optimization controls, integration comparisons and the comparison
example. The oracle's 16 engine function bodies match the frozen baseline
(two require rustfmt normalization); `noteskin-oracle-source-audit.json` records
their hashes and the import/visibility adaptations needed for an external test.

Compiler version 30 changes the source/cache identity. A regression verifies
that a version-29 cache is rebuilt, remains on disk unchanged, and the new
bundle is subsequently reused. Differential checks assert the exact 29-to-30
transition before comparing all payload fields and serialization round trips.

`noteskin-cutover-oracle-fixed-noteskin-linux-debug` passed 311 tests. The further
`noteskin-callbacks-complete-noteskin-linux-debug` run passed 312 tests with source
hashes unchanged: 299 unit tests, five existing integration tests and eight
migration tests. Comparisons cover all 26 bundled skins, six authored fixtures,
seven regression fixtures under both games (including the existing explicit
pump rejection), fallback closures, color resources, errors and property
metamethods. The added byte-for-byte callback fixture test also runs against the
production Rust entry point. New production tests retain the historical callback/alias coverage,
force GC during callbacks and aliases, check panic propagation and destruction,
and verify the old safe-library restrictions. The Rust adapter now removes
`debug` from globals and loaded modules and preserves the disabled C-loader
behavior. Historical C-bridge panic transport tests remain dev-oracle-only;
the production Rust host contract propagates panics to Rust and drops the VM.

The first cutover run failed because the external oracle needed a private
comment parser helper and a module alias. The helper was copied from the frozen
implementation; no failing test was removed. The strict noteskin Clippy run
reports existing warnings in unchanged code and historical test controls; its
raw log is `noteskin-cutover-clippy-linux.log`. Ordinary Clippy passed with no
diagnostics in the new adapter or migration tests; the source comparison,
diagnostic classification, format check and exact lint scope are recorded in
`noteskin-cutover-lint-results.json`. Final downstream/application
checks and controlled release performance comparisons remain pending.

## Rendered application baseline

`baseline-rendered-dreaming-windows` preserves a completed run of the normal
